items: Know the situation of the thorax.
Know its constituents: bones, joints, muscles, vessels and nerves.
C. Constitution of the chest wall

pages.title: General Anatomy and Limits of the Thorax

blocks.text: The thorax is the region that occupies the upper part of the trunk, located between the neck at the top and the abdomen at the bottom.
Deformable, it participates in respiratory movements. It is surrounded by a musculoskeletal wall.
It surrounds and protects the main organs of the circulatory and respiratory systems, including the heart, lungs and large vessels.
The thorax is cylindrical in shape in the newborn and slightly flattened and conical in the adult, with a lower base.
The thorax consists of a wall and a cavity.

rows: An upper thoracic aperture located at the base of the neck, through which the thorax communicates with the neck.
A wider lower thoracic aperture closed by the diaphragm.

blocks.text: The diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity from the main abdominal viscera.
C. Constitution of the Chest Wall
The chest wall is lined internally by the endothoracic fascia and is made up of skeletal and muscular elements.

items: Laterally: twelve pairs of ribs, with the intercostal muscles contained in the intercostal spaces, and the costal cartilages.

blocks.text: The sternum is a flat, median, unpaired and symmetrical subcutaneous bone. It is located in the anterosuperior part of the rib cage and contributes to the attachment of the shoulder girdle.

items: Inferiorly: the tip of the sternum.

blocks.text: The sternum provides attachment for several muscles. It has two surfaces: an anterior or ventral surface and a posterior or dorsal surface. It has three borders: one superior border and two lateral borders, which are irregular.
Laterally, it articulates with the ribs through the costal cartilages. Superiorly and laterally, it articulates with the clavicles.
The manubrium is the upper part of the sternum. It is thick, wide and trapezoid-shaped, with a broad upper base.

items: The jugular notch, or sternal fork, is located in its upper and middle part.
On either side of the jugular notch are the clavicular notches, which articulate with the clavicles through saddle joints.
Laterally and superiorly is the first costal notch, which articulates with the first costal cartilage.
Laterally and inferiorly is a half-notch for the upper half of the second costal cartilage.

blocks.text: The body of the sternum is narrow and elongated. It presents transverse striations corresponding to the lines of fusion of the six sternebrae, which are the segmental elements of the sternum.

items: Superiorly: a half-articular notch for the lower half of the second costal cartilage.
Costal notches for the third, fourth, fifth and sixth costal cartilages.
Inferiorly: a half-notch for the upper half of the seventh costal cartilage.

blocks.text: The angle of Louis, or sternal angle, is located between the manubrium and the body of the sternum. It measures approximately 15°.
The xiphoid process forms the inferior part of the sternum. It is cartilaginous and has a variable shape, which may be tapered, widened or bifid.
At its upper lateral ends, it presents a half-articular notch with the lower half of the seventh costal cartilage.
The ribs are flat, paired and asymmetrical bones that form most of the rib cage. There are twelve pairs of ribs numbered from superior to inferior.

rows: Articulate directly with the sternum through their costal cartilages.
Their costal cartilages unite with the cartilage of the seventh rib.
Free anteriorly and do not attach to the sternum.

blocks.text: The eighth through twelfth ribs are therefore called asternal ribs.

items: The length of the ribs increases from the first to the seventh and then decreases from the eighth to the twelfth.
The width of the true ribs increases from posterior to anterior and reaches its maximum at the anterior end.
The false ribs are wider in their middle part.
The first rib is the widest and the second rib is the narrowest.
The eighth, ninth and tenth ribs are wider than the ribs above them.

blocks.text: From the thoracic spine, a rib runs obliquely forward and downward. This obliquity becomes more pronounced toward the inferior ribs.
A typical rib is a flat, elongated bone shaped approximately like an italic S. It is medially concave and consists of a curved body and two ends.
The body is flattened transversely and concave medially. It initially runs laterally and posteriorly, forming the anterior costal angle, then changes direction and forms the posterior angle.

items: Two borders: a thick superior border and a thinner inferior border.
The inferior border contains the costal groove, which houses the intercostal neurovascular bundle.

blocks.text: The dorsal end articulates with the vertebral column and consists of the head, neck and costal tubercle.
The head has two articular facets, superior and inferior, separated by a crest corresponding to the intervertebral disc.
The neck is a short, flattened region separating the head from the tubercle.

The costal tubercle is located between the neck and the body of the rib. It contains a non-articular part and an articular part that articulates with the facet of the transverse process of the corresponding vertebra.
The ventral end continues with the costal cartilage.

rows: Smaller than the other ribs; flattened from superior to inferior; has superior and inferior surfaces; lacks a costal groove; its head has a single articular facet for T1.
Has an oblique orientation intermediate between the first and third ribs; lacks a costal groove.
The head has a single facet that articulates with T10.
Lack a costal tubercle and neck. Each articulates only with the corresponding thoracic vertebra.

pages.title: Thoracic Spine and Joints of the Thorax

blocks.text: There are twelve thoracic vertebrae, which articulate with the ribs.

rows: Cylindrical, with four costal facets on its posterior part: superior and inferior.
Directed obliquely outward and backward and contain a costal articular facet, except at T11 and T12.

blocks.text: The costocorporeal joint unites the head of a rib with two adjacent vertebral bodies.
The costotransverse joint unites the costal tubercle with the transverse process of the vertebra of the same number.
Costochondral joints connect the ribs to their costal cartilages.
Interchondral joints unite the sixth, seventh and eighth costal cartilages.
There are seven pairs of chondrosternal joints, which unite the sternum with the costal cartilages.
With the exception of the first and seventh, each consists of two arthrodial joints.

pages.title: Muscles and Functional Anatomy of the Thorax

blocks.text: The movements of the rib cage are continuous and accompany breathing. They essentially result from movements of the costovertebral joints.
The sternocostal and interchondral joints are the sites of small sliding movements.
